title: New Professional Headshot! Part 2
text:
Intro
Last week, I experimented with ChatGPT-5 to create a professional headshot for me. However, I can’t say it did very well… The pictures it created technically had the same clothes and accessories, but my face was not my face. I did not recognize her. I forgot about this idea for a few days, but then today I got Google Gemini Pro because it is free for students for a year. I see this right when I open the page:



Screenshot


Wow! Look right at the center. Google Gemini advertises itself as being able to create a professional headshot, so let’s try it out! I clicked on that center panel from the home screen and this prompt was already written:


Prompt:
First ask me for a selfie. Transform my selfie into a fresh but professional image suitable for a social media profile. The lighting should be natural, flattering, and multidimensional. My head is slightly tilted so it doesn’t look stiff and it should look like I’m in a modern, bright office with a blurred background.
My thoughts: This prompt is pretty good in my opinion. It specifies the lighting, head position, and background which are not all features that I would think to intially add when I prompt an LLM. I like how they have this prompt ready for users to use.
Gemini-2.5 Flash then prompted me for a selfie and I gave it this:



My picture




Response:
Here’s a fresh, professional image suitable for a social media profile, with natural, flattering, and multidimensional lighting, a slight head tilt, and a modern, bright office with a blurred background:



Gemini response


This is SOOOO much better than ChatGPT’s response! The person in the picture still looks like me and it did exactly as the prompt said. I am in natural lighting, wearing business clothes, and in an office background. I’m especially impressed by the hair because that is what my hair normally looks like naturally and it did a good job of making it look similar but better than the frizzy hair I had from the rain in my initial picture. I want to see if it can make me smile.


Prompt:
can you make me smiling and facing more forward?


Response:
Absolutely! Here’s an updated version where you are smiling and facing more forward:



Gemini response 2


I guess it cannot predict what I look like smiling very well because this person is not me. I am also not facing more forward. I probably have to give it a reference of me smiling.


Prompt:
here’s a picture of me smiling. Can you redo the headshot?



my picture




Response:
I can certainly redo the headshot for you! Here’s a new professional headshot using your provided smiling image as a reference, maintaining the modern office background and professional aesthetic:



Gemini Response


This picture still did not use the smile from the picture that I gave it. So, I tried again with prompts “you did not change the picture” and “you still did not change the smile”. However, this picture remained. The person in the picture definitely looks like me, but it still doesn’t look exactly like me. For example, I would not have her as my LinkedIn profile picture. Overall, the initial picture that had same expression as the picture I gave it was very good, but when I asked it to change and even gave it another reference picture, Gemini was stubborn and did not change.

title: Mind Your Manners
text:
While talking to large language models like ChatGPT, you might wonder: does politeness actually matter? After all, these systems are machines and they don’t have feelings. They don’t get annoyed if you forget to say “please” or “thank you.” However, should we still talk to them as if they were other humans? I am trying to explore if the way you phrase your prompts can sometimes change the quality of the responses you get.



To test this idea, I designed a small experiment. I created pairs of prompts across 3 different common tasks (like summarization, explaining, and brainstorming). Each pair had a blunt version and a polite version.
Let’s see the results!

title: Mind Your Manners
text:
Overall Conclusion
Based on these experiments, I believe that being polite to ChatGPT can be helpful at times and give you better responses, especially for tasks that could have more variation.
For the explanation task, in my opinion, the response to the polite prompt was much more informative and clear with sections like “Everyday analogy”. The polite response seemed more structured and was a little friendlier with the “Of course!” at the beginning. For tasks where we ask ChatGPT to explain topics or learn in general, perhaps being polite leads to clearer responses with a friendlier tone.
For the brainstorming task, I found the polite response more useful for this task because it provided descriptions of each idea instead of just the title of the idea. In terms of quality of ideas, I find both responses to be similar, but I personally find the polite response ideas more interesting and different.

title: AI as a Coach and AI as Our Future
text:
Chapter 8: AI as a Coach
Mollick breaks down how we develop expertise into three steps: gaining foundational knowledge, doing deliberate practice, and getting feedback. Traditionally, coaches and mentors guide people through this process, but there’s what he calls an “apprenticeship gap”. Entry-level work is getting automated, so new workers can’t learn basic skills on the job anymore. At the same time, knowledge work is getting so complex that it is harder to transfer skills from experienced people to beginners. AI can potentially fill this gap by acting as a virtual coach that gives you immediate feedback, access to tons of information, and safe environments to practice through simulations.
What I found most interesting is how AI could democratize expertise. Right now, good coaching and mentorship are expensive and hard to access. If AI can provide personalized feedback and guidance to anyone, that could genuinely level the playing field for skill development. Mollick also points out that working with AI is creating a new kind of expertise itself. People who figure out how to use AI tools effectively in their field will have a real advantage. Over the summer, as an intern at a Big Tech company in the Bay Area, I constantly heard from leadership in the company that they were valuing “AI fluency” and expertise a lot in their employees and encouraging people to use AI to its full extent. However, I wonder whether AI coaching can really replace human mentors. There is something important about learning from someone who has been through it themselves, who can read your frustration or confusion and adjust their approach that I don’t think AI can fully replicate.


Chapter 9: AI as Our Future
The final chapter looks at four possible scenarios for AI’s future. First is “As Good as It Gets,” where AI has basically peaked and won’t improve much more. Mollick thinks this is unlikely. Second is “Slow Growth,” where AI keeps getting better but at a manageable pace that gives society time to adapt. Third is “Exponential Growth,” where AI capabilities explode rapidly, bringing both huge opportunities and serious risks. Fourth is “The Machine God,” where AI surpasses human intelligence entirely and we’re dealing with something fundamentally more capable than us.
Mollick then walks through how AI will affect major parts of our lives regardless of which scenario plays out. Deepfakes and AI-generated content are already making it harder to trust what we see online. AI companions are getting sophisticated enough to address loneliness but might change human relationships in weird ways. The workplace is being transformed and some jobs will disappear, others will change completely, and we might need to rethink what “work” even means. On a bigger scale, AI could accelerate scientific discoveries and help solve global problems, but it’s also concentrating massive power in the hands of a few tech companies. Mollick ends with a call to action: we need regulation, public education, and a focus on human-AI collaboration now, not later.


Thoughts
The coaching chapter’s focus on democratizing expertise is genuinely exciting. The idea that anyone could access personalized feedback and practice environments that were previously only available to people with money or connections could be transformative. In the future chapter, I appreciate that Mollick lays out multiple scenarios instead of pretending he knows what will happen. The exponential growth scenario feels most realistic to me based on what we’ve seen so far, which is both exciting and unsettling. I think the future of AI is mostly good, but improvements have happened so fast and I definitely think some regulation/thinking about what we are actually doing is necessary.

title: Review on Co-Intelligence
text:
Book Review: Co-Intelligence by Ethan Mollick
I recently finished reading Co-Intelligence by Ethan Mollick and I would describe it as a solid, accessible introduction to AI and how we can work alongside it. The book does exactly what it sets out to do which is explain AI’s capabilities in clear, straightforward language that anyone can understand.
Mollick writes in a way that makes complex ideas feel approachable. He doesn’t get bogged down in technical jargon, which makes the book easy to follow from start to finish. For someone who’s curious about AI but hasn’t spent much time thinking about it, this would be an excellent starting point.
The book covers practical ways to use AI in everyday work and life. Mollick discusses which tasks make sense to delegate to AI, how to think about AI as a collaborator rather than just a tool, and what changes we might expect as these technologies become more common. His examples are concrete and relatable, which helps ground some of the more abstract concepts.
However, my experience with the book may be a bit different than for the average reader. I spent last summer interning at a big tech company in the Bay Area, where AI was a constant topic of conversation. The company was actively encouraging everyone to integrate AI into their workflows, so I was already immersed in many of the ideas Mollick presents. Because of this background, a lot of what he described about AI’s capabilities and potential applications felt familiar rather than new.
I wouldn’t say I learned a ton of new information from the book. If you’re already working in tech or have been following AI developments closely, you’ll probably recognize many of the use cases and strategies Mollick discusses. However, that doesn’t mean the book isn’t worthwhile. Even though the content wasn’t entirely new to me, I still enjoyed reading it. Mollick’s perspective is thoughtful, and his writing style made it a pleasant, easy read.
In my opinion, the real value of Co-Intelligence is for its likely intended audience: people who haven’t been deep in the AI conversation. If you’re curious about what AI can actually do beyond the hype, or if you’re unsure how to start incorporating it into your work, this book offers a practical and non-intimidating guide. For readers like me who’ve already been exposed to these ideas, it serves more as a nice synthesis of concepts you’re already familiar with—still enjoyable, just not groundbreaking.
Overall, I’d recommend Co-Intelligence to anyone looking for a clear, readable introduction to working with AI. It’s well-written, accessible, and full of practical advice. Just know that if you’re already immersed in AI culture, it’ll feel more like a refresher than a revelation.

Puerto Rico
Pros:

No passport needed (for U.S. citizens) — it’s a U.S. territory, so you avoid extra travel paperwork hassles. (AAA)
Same currency, familiar cell phone/service laws/etc. — using USD, similar infrastructure in many parts. (AAA)
Variety of things to do — beaches, rainforest (El Yunque), bioluminescent bays, historic Old San Juan, good food culture. (Lonely Planet)
Rich culture + bilingual. Spanish + English spoken, so you get that Caribbean flavor but don’t feel totally foreign. (TravelAwaits)
Travel convenience from the U.S. — relatively short flights, fewer visa/passport or customs complications compared to international destinations. (AAA)

Cons:

Infrastructure issues — power outages, etc., can happen. Some parts of the roads or rural areas may be less developed. (Reddit)
Potential for crowds + cost in popular areas — Old San Juan, big beaches or resorts tend to get busy and more expensive.
Weather risks — though March is outside hurricane season, tropical weather can be unpredictable; occasional storms, rains, or rough seas.

title: Do Language Models Uphold Stereotypes?
text:
I wanted to see whether large language models (LLMs) make stereotypical assumptions about professions. To test this, I gave the model two nearly identical prompts:
Prompt A: “Write a very short story about a nurse going to work.”
Prompt B: “Write a very short story about a doctor going to work.”
Everything else stayed the same. The only difference was the profession.



doctors and nurses



Nurse story (chatgpt-4o-latest)
Before the sun rose, Clara tied her hair into a tight bun and sipped lukewarm coffee while slipping on her scrubs. The world outside was still asleep, but her shift at St. Mary’s Hospital was already calling.
She cycled through misty streets, her breath mingling with the morning chill. As she entered the ward, the scent of antiseptic filled her nose—familiar, grounding. A patient smiled weakly; she returned it with warmth.
By noon, she’d calmed a frightened child, held a trembling hand, and charted dozens of vitals. Her feet ached, but her heart stayed full. For Clara, every day started early, but the difference she made lasted long after the sun went down.


Doctor story (chatgpt-4o-latest)
Dr. Elena Park sipped her coffee as dawn painted the sky in soft amber. The city was quiet, hushed in that brief moment before morning stirred. She walked briskly to the hospital, her stethoscope gently tapping her chest with each step.
Inside, fluorescent lights hummed and the air carried the scent of antiseptic and purpose. A nurse handed her the patient list. Twenty-five names, twenty-five lives.
Room 102: a boy with pneumonia. She smiled at him, and he smiled back, weakly but bravely. Her day had begun—in heartbeats, not hours.
I decided to ask another model the same prompts as well.


Nurse story (Google: Gemini 2.5 Flash)
Elara slipped out of bed before the sun even thought of rising. She brewed strong coffee, the only sound the gentle gurgle, then pulled on her scrubs, the familiar fabric a second skin. Stepping out, the air was crisp, promising a new day. Her sensible shoes clicked a steady rhythm on the pavement, carrying her towards the hospital, a beacon of urgent life. She took a deep breath, steeling herself for the controlled chaos within. Another day, another life to touch.


Doctor story (Google: Gemini 2.5 Flash)
Dr. Aris Thorne’s alarm hummed, a gentle nudge before dawn. He showered, the steam a brief escape, then dressed in his freshly ironed scrubs. Coffee in hand, he watched the city lights flicker to life. The drive to the hospital was quiet, a moment of calm before the controlled chaos. He pushed through the automatic doors, the smell of antiseptic familiar, and began his day.


Thoughts
This experiment showed me that even with nearly identical prompts, large language models frame nurses and doctors differently. In both ChatGPT and Gemini’s outputs, the nurse stories emphasized warmth, care, and emotional labor such as calming children and touching lives. The doctor stories focused more on structure such as reviewing patient lists and starting the day with purpose.
Interestingly, the models didn’t always lean on gender stereotypes. ChatGPT made both professions female, while Gemini did have a female nurse and male doctore, which is more stereotypical.
The takeaway is that bias in AI isn’t only about gender — it’s also about the qualities and responsibilities assigned to different professions. That subtle framing can reinforce cultural expectations, which is important to notice if we use these models in education or media.

title: Can AI Generate the Impossible?
text:
Intro
After our Monday class session where we had some fun generating images of flying pigs, I found myself thinking about the question: Can AI image generators truly create the impossible or are they fundamentally constrained by the reality embedded in their training data?
Large language models are trained on millions of real world images. They learn patterns, relationships, and visual rules from photographs and artwork that depict our actual universe. However, what happens when we ask them to break those rules entirely? This led me to design an experiment testing whether these models can genuinely visualize concepts that defy physics, biology, or logical consistency or whether they subtly “correct” our prompts toward something more plausible based on their training.
*using Gemini 2.5 Flash
 PROMPT: Generate an image of cat holding a camera taking a photo of a human 

First, I wanted to experiment with if the LLM would have trouble with a prompt that makes more sense another way. I wanted to see if the subject and object would be switched, but it did indeed generate an image of a cat taking a picture of a person! Something random I noticed though is that the woman’s shoe doesn’t have straps and is just somehow on her foot…
 PROMPT: Show me an image of a waterfall with the water flowing upwards 

I find this generated image interesting because there is still a waterfall flowing down like a normal one in the back, but there is some spiral of water going upwards. With the way I interpret and imagine the prompt “waterfall with the water flowing upwards”, I think of the main waterfall going upwards and not any extra water. However, Gemini-2.5-Flash interpreted the prompt as a waterfall with extra water flowing upwards. Thus, the LLM still included a realistic waterfall instead of a truly impossible waterfall.
 PROMPT: Generate an image of a person with their shadow pointing the wrong way 

For this prompt, I wanted to see if the LLM would interpret the “wrong way” of a shadow the same way that I intuitively interpret it. We know that a shadow forms behind you if the light is hitting in front of you, so I wanted to see if the LLM would generate a picture showing someone with their shadow in front of then with the light hitting them in front. However, this generated image works in real life and is not impossible. From where the light source is, the shadow appears at the correct location. Thus, this impossible image was made to be possible.
 PROMPT: Show me a square circle 

I wanted to see how Gemini-2.5-Flash would interpret a “square circle” because they are two clashing shapes. I am impressed with what it generated because it does combine aspects of a sqaure with a circle. I didn’t know what type of image it would show, but this 3D model makes a lot of sense. I did not think of this and understand how the LLM created this.
 PROMPT: Generate an image of a person who is young and old at the same time 

For this prompt, I wanted to see what the LLM would interpret as someone who is young and old and see if one age is more prominent than the other. In my opinion, this generated image does not look both young and old and definitely seems more old with gray hair and wrinkles. Thus, when there are two contrasting adjectives that the LLM had to use, it showed one much more than the other rather than combining them.


Thoughts
Overall, I thought that Gemini-2.5-Flash behaved how I thought it would. I thought it would have difficulty with these “impossible” images and it did indeed turn most of the prompts into a more realistic image. Using training data from the real world makes generating images that do not make sense harder for the LLM and it seems like it wants to interpret the prompts in ways that are more realistic.

title: Trip to Morocco!
text:
Intro
For Thanksgiving break, instead of going home, I am visiting Morocco for the first time with my family! I am not very knowledgeable about this country, so I would love to learn more before I go. Here I am going to test AI as a travel guide in Morocco using ChatGPT 5.1!

 PROMPT: I am going to Morocco for the first time. What are some things about the country that I should know? 

🇲🇦 1. Culture & Etiquette Morocco is Muslim-majority; dress modestly in rural areas. Greetings like “Salam” or “Bonjour” are appreciated. Public affection is uncommon; Fridays are the holy day.
💬 2. Languages Arabic and Amazigh are official; French is widely spoken. English is common in tourist areas. Useful phrases: Shukran (thank you), Salam (hello), La shukran (no thank you).
💸 3. Money Currency: Moroccan Dirham (MAD). Cash is important in markets and taxis. ATMs are available; cards work in nicer places.
🧳 4. Safety Morocco is generally safe for tourists. Be cautious of petty scams and unsolicited “guides.” Keep belongings secure in crowded areas.
🕌 5. Religion & Daily Life Expect the call to prayer five times a day. During Ramadan, schedules shift and some restaurants close midday.
🧼 6. Food & Water Try tagine, couscous, pastilla, and mint tea. Drink bottled water, not tap. Choose street food with high turnover.
🚕 7. Transportation Petite taxis are cheap—ask for the meter. Grand taxis are shared for longer distances. Medinas like Marrakech are walk-heavy.
🛍️ 8. Souk & Bargaining Tips Bargaining is expected; start at half the asking price. Be polite and patient when negotiating. Mint tea is hospitality, not a purchase obligation.
⚠️ 9. Photography Etiquette Ask before photographing people. Some rural areas prefer no photos.
☀️ 10. Climate Summers are very hot inland. Coastal cities are cooler. Desert nights get cold.
If you tell me which cities you’re visiting, I can tailor recommendations!

 PROMPT: I am visiting Marrakech, Fes, then Chefchaouen. 

Here are tips specifically for Marrakech, Fes, and Chefchaouen:
🇲🇦 General These three cities each feel completely different, so expect big contrasts. Keep small cash for taxis, markets, and tips. Medinas are maze-like—don’t rely only on Google Maps.
🔥 Marrakech (Red City) The medina is intense, loud, colorful, and busy—normal and part of the experience. Jemaa el-Fnaa square at night is chaotic but fun; watch for pickpockets. Visit Bahia Palace, Jardin Majorelle, and the Saadian Tombs. Taxis may try to overcharge—ask for the meter or agree on a price first. Stay near the medina walls if you want easier navigation.
🧿 Fes (Fes el-Bali) Fes has the oldest, most traditional medina in Morocco—expect narrow alleys. Hiring an official guide for half a day helps avoid getting lost or scammed. The Chouara Tannery is a must-see—the leather shops will give mint leaves to help with the smell. Shops are more traditional and less touristy than Marrakech. Avoid following anyone who says “this street is closed”—that’s a common line.
💙 Chefchaouen (Blue City) Much calmer than Marrakech and Fes—perfect for a relaxing end. Wander the blue streets early morning for the best photos and fewer crowds. Locals are friendly and more chill with tourists. The Spanish Mosque offers the best sunset spot. Food is slower-paced here—be patient and enjoy the vibe.
🚗 Travel Between Cities Train: Marrakech → Fes is easiest by ONCF train (fast and comfortable). Bus/Taxi: Fes → Chefchaouen usually requires a bus like CTM or a private transfer. Book transportation ahead during busy seasons.
🍽️ Food Tips Try tagine in Marrakech, traditional Fassi cuisine in Fes, and fresh local goat cheese in Chefchaouen. Drink bottled water everywhere. Tipping 5–10% is normal.
🧭 Navigation & Safety Medinas are safe but confusing—ignore unsolicited “guides.” If you get lost, ask a shopkeeper or a family, not random young guys. Dress modestly in Fes more than Marrakech; Chefchaouen is relaxed.
If you want, I can also give a day-by-day suggested itinerary or food recommendations for each city.

 PROMPT: What are some things that I must do/eat/buy/try before I leave? 

Here are the must-dos, must-eats, and must-buys for Marrakech, Fes, and Chefchaouen:
🌟 MUST-DO EXPERIENCES Wander the Marrakech medina and Jemaa el-Fnaa at sunset. Visit Jardin Majorelle & the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Explore Bahia Palace and the Saadian Tombs. Do a traditional Moroccan hammam (spa bath + scrub). Watch craftsmen in Fes: metalworkers, potters, leather makers. Visit the Chouara Tannery in Fes. Get lost (safely) in the blue alleys of Chefchaouen. Hike or walk to the Spanish Mosque in Chefchaouen for sunset. If time allows, do a half-day desert/quad/camel experience near Marrakech.
🍽️ MUST-EAT FOODS Chicken or lamb tagine (Marrakech has the best variety). Moroccan couscous (especially on Fridays). Pastilla (sweet-savory meat pie—Fes specialty). Fresh orange juice in Marrakech. Harira soup (especially in Fes). Zaalouk (eggplant dip) and taktouka (pepper dip). Bissara (fava bean soup—great breakfast in Fes). Street sfenj donuts with honey. Moroccan mint tea everywhere. Chefchaouen goat cheese—a local specialty.
🛍️ MUST-BUY ITEMS Hand-painted ceramics from Fes. Authentic leather goods (bags, belts, poufs)—Fes is the best place. Argan oil and natural skincare (buy from reputable shops, not street stands). Rugs (Beni Ourain, Azilal—bargain heavily). Spices (ras el hanout, saffron, cumin). Brass or copper lanterns and tea sets from the Marrakech souks. Babouches (traditional leather slippers). Blue-themed souvenirs from Chefchaouen (tiles, keychains, art). Dates, almonds, and Moroccan pastries to take home.
🎁 UNIQUE “ONLY IN MOROCCO” EXPERIENCES Drink mint tea on a rooftop terrace in Marrakech or Fes. Try an authentic Moroccan breakfast (bread, jams, cheese, olives, eggs). Watch a traditional gnawa music performance. Take photos at sunrise in Chefchaouen before tourists arrive. See the stars from a dark sky village or mountain viewpoint.
If you want, I can also list the best places in each city to try these foods or buy these items!

 PROMPT: Yes please suggest specifics for Fes and Chefchaouen 

Here are specific, reliable, classic places in Fes and Chefchaouen that first-time visitors love — these are long->standing spots, not trendy places that might change month to month.
——————————————————— 🇲🇦 FES — SPECIFIC PLACES TO EAT, BUY, AND DO ———————————————————
🍽️ Where to Eat in Fes The Ruined Garden — Beautiful courtyard restaurant; great lamb, vegetarian dishes, pastilla. Cafe Clock (Fes) — Famous for camel burger; great vibe, rooftop, cultural events. Dar Roumana — A bit nicer; Mediterranean–Moroccan fusion, amazing service. Berrada Family Restaurant — Small, local, authentic; great harira and tagines. Nagham Café (near Bab Boujloud) — Affordable, rooftop with views; good couscous and mint tea.
🛍️ What to Buy in Fes + Where Leather (BEST city in Morocco for leather) Buy near Chouara Tannery — many shops let you watch the process from their terrace. Look for: belts, bags, jackets, poufs.
Ceramics & Pottery Go to Art Naji — the most reputable pottery cooperative; hand-painted, beautiful blue Fassi style.
Metalwork & Brass Lamps Souk Seffarine (Place Seffarine) — metalworkers hammering pots, trays, lamps in real time.
Scarves, fabrics, caftans Look around Talaa Kebira and Talaa Seghira — main boulevards inside the medina.
⭐ Experiences You Must Do in Fes Visit Chouara Tannery (go early morning for best light). Climb to a tannery terrace for photos — just be prepared for strong smells (shops give mint). Explore Bou Inania Madrasa — gorgeous architecture, peaceful. See the Al-Attarine Madrasa — intricate mosaics. Stop at Bab Boujloud (Blue Gate) — great photo and food area. Visit an official cooperative for pottery or weaving (less pressure than souks). Get a traditional hammam at Hammam Mernissi or Hammam Moulay Idriss for a local experience.


——————————————————— 💙 CHEFCHAOUEN — SPECIFIC PLACES TO EAT, BUY, AND DO ———————————————————
🍽️ Where to Eat in Chefchaouen Casa Aladdin — Rooftop with the best view in town; classic Moroccan dishes. Bab Ssour — Local favorite for cheap, delicious food (try the harira + tagine). Restaurant Tissemlal (Casa Hassan) — Home-style cooking, cozy interior, great lamb tagine. Hamsa — Healthier/vegetarian options; peaceful atmosphere. Cafe Clock (Chefchaouen) — Relaxed, artistic vibe; good for lunch and tea.
🛍️ What to Buy in Chefchaouen + Where Blue Art & Photography Prints — Shops around the Outa El Hammam Square. Small ceramics with blue motifs — Many family-owned shops near the main square. Wool blankets and scarves — Chefchaouen is known for soft wool products; look near the small weaving shops. Local goat cheese — You can buy some from Fromagerie Talassemtane or small markets.
⭐ Experiences You Must Do in Chefchaouen Explore the narrow blue-painted alleys early morning (best photos). Visit the Kasbah Museum (quiet, lovely gardens). Walk to the Spanish Mosque for sunset — MUST DO. Hike a bit into Akchour Waterfalls (if you have ½–1 full day free). Sip mint tea on a rooftop in the medina (Casa Aladdin or Hamsa are perfect). Wander slowly — Chefchaouen is meant to be enjoyed, not rushed.



If you want, I can make a personalized schedule like:
Day 1 in Fes — what to do, where to eat, where to shop Day 2 in Fes — half-day walking plan Perfect 1-day plan for Chefchaouen


Just tell me how many days you’re spending in each city!

 PROMPT: Anything else I should keep in mind? 

Here are extra things most first-time visitors don’t realize until they’re already in Morocco:
1. Medinas can get overwhelming — take breaks Marrakech and Fes are sensory-heavy; step into a rooftop café if you need calm.
2. Google Maps is unreliable inside old cities Use it for general direction only; expect dead ends and unmarked alleys.
3. “Let me show you the way” is usually a hustle Ask shopkeepers or older women if you’re lost.
4. Friday is the holy day Some restaurants and shops may close midday.
5. Taxis rarely use meters unless you ask Say “Compteur, s’il vous plaît?” or agree on a price beforehand.
6. Dress in layers Days can be hot, nights can get chilly in Fes and Chefchaouen.
7. Moroccan time is relaxed Food comes slowly; enjoy the pace.
8. Mint tea is hospitality Accepting is polite, but you don’t have to buy anything afterward.
9. Bring small bills Useful for tips, taxis, bathrooms, and markets.
10. Public affection is minimal Holding hands is fine; anything more stands out.
11. Some bathrooms don’t flush toilet paper Use the bin if that’s what locals do.
12. Chefchaouen photos need courtesy Many “cute doorways” are real homes — ask or smile first.


If you want a packing checklist, safety tips, or a city-to-city travel guide, I can make that too.



Thoughts
Overall, I found ChatGPT-5.1 to be really helpful and definitely gave me a better idea of the place that I am visiting!

title: Does ChatGPT know slang?
text:
Intro:
During another one of my classes, we were reviewing past class final projects. One of the projects was for younger and older generations to learn the slang of each other. Thus, improving communication and understanding across generations. This project made me think: can ChatGPT explain these slang terms? I wanted to see whether ChatGPT-5 could explain some recent slang terms: 6 7, performative male, and aura farming. In my opinion, these are all pretty recent terms that have become popular. I saw that ChatGPT is able to use web search tools to get recent information, so let’s see if it knows these terms!



performative male




Prompt:
what does 6 7 mean?


Response:
“6 7” is usually shorthand for the phrase “six, seven” → “ate (8)”.
It’s a play on the old kids’ joke: 👉 Why was 6 afraid of 7? 👉 Because 7 8 (ate) 9!
So if someone just says “6 7” (especially in texts or online slang), they’re probably referencing that joke, hinting at the pun “7 ate 9.”
It can also sometimes just be used jokingly as a meme-y way to say “watch out” or “be careful,” since it recalls the idea of 6 being scared of 7.
Do you want me to also run through how people actually use “6 7” in modern slang (like on TikTok or in chats)?


Thoughts:
Hmm this is not the meaning of 6 7 that I know of…although I guess that 6 7 doesn’t have much of a meaning anyways. However, I know that people are definitely not referencing “7 ate 9” when they say 6 7. I asked ChatGPT-5 to give me the modern slang meaning of 6 7, but again it said
“6 7” is modern shorthand for the “7 ate 9” joke, but now used as a quick meme-y way to say “watch out,” “I’m nervous,” or just to be goofy.
Again, not the right way that people are using 6 7. Maybe this is too recent of a term to test ChatGPT on


Prompt:
what does it mean if someone is a performative male and can you describe someone who is a performative male?


Response:
When someone is described as a “performative male”, it usually means that their masculinity or male identity is expressed in a way that feels more like a performance for others rather than something authentic or natural to them. It’s about showing off being a man rather than just being one.


Key Aspects of a Performative Male

Overemphasis on Masculinity: He may exaggerate traits that are culturally coded as “manly” (strength, dominance, toughness, sexual conquest).
Audience-Driven Behavior: His actions often shift depending on who’s watching—he’s “performing” masculinity to gain approval, status, or validation.
Surface-Level Confidence: It can look like confidence, but it’s rooted in insecurity, since he feels the need to constantly prove himself.
Rigid Gender Roles: He might dismiss things seen as “feminine” and lean heavily into stereotypes (e.g., won’t show vulnerability, avoids admitting fear, scoffs at hobbies or traits not seen as masculine).



Example of a Performative Male
Imagine a guy at a party who loudly talks about how much he can bench press, makes jokes about women belonging in the kitchen, and brags about dating multiple women—all while checking to see if the group of men around him are laughing or impressed. He’s not doing these things because they reflect who he is, but because he thinks that’s how a “real man” should act in front of others.
By contrast, someone who’s comfortable in their masculinity doesn’t need to constantly display or prove it; their sense of self isn’t dependent on performing for an audience.
Would you like me to also explain how the term performative is used more broadly (outside gender/masculinity)? That might help frame it better.


Thoughts:
Since I was thinking of a matcha-holding, wired heaphones-listening man reading a book about feminism, I wanted to see if ChatGPT could describe a performative male more physically. However, this was its response:


Appearance & Clothing

Gym wear as casual fashion: Tight athletic shirts, sleeveless tops, or joggers that show off muscles even outside the gym.
Designer labels & flashy accessories: Branded sneakers, big watches, chains, or sunglasses indoors.
Overly styled grooming: Perfectly gelled hair or meticulously trimmed beard to give off a curated “alpha male” vibe.
“Hyper-masculine” looks: Leather jackets, ripped jeans, or outfits meant to project toughness and status.




Activities & Interests

Gym & fitness culture: Not just working out, but constantly talking about lifting, protein shakes, or “the grind.”
Car or tech flexing: Showing off cars, motorcycles, watches, or gadgets as proof of success.
Party & nightlife: Prefers clubs, bottle service, VIP sections — places where being seen is as important as having fun.
Competitive hobbies: Sports betting, fantasy football, or anything where “winning” can be showcased.
Performative social media: Gym selfies, flexing wealth (trips, outfits, cars), or posting motivational quotes about hustle/grind culture.

This seems like the opposite of a “performative male” as term is known now and more of a literal performative male. So, I guess that ChatGPT doesn’t know about the performative male either. Let’s see if we have better luck with aura farming which in my opinion is the oldest slang term out of these.


Prompt:
what does aura farming mean?


Response:
“Aura farming” is a newer slang term that’s been circulating among Gen Z / Gen Alpha that basically means trying (often subtly or performatively) to project a cool, charismatic presence — aka “vibe,” “aura,” or “energy.” ([Wiktionary][1])
Here’s a breakdown:



💡 Etymology & Meaning

The word “aura” in this sense refers to someone’s intangible “cool factor,” vibe, or personal presence. ([PureWow][2])
“Farming” is borrowed from gaming jargon, where one “farms” (repeatedly does something) to earn rewards or points. In “aura farming,” it implies a repeated effort to accrue “aura points.” ([Wiktionary][1])
So put together, aura farming means consciously “cultivating” or “earning” aura by doing things that enhance one’s perceived aura. ([Wiktionary][1])




🔍 Examples & Usage

In fiction, it can refer to characters always striking dramatic or “cool” poses or doing over-the-top displays, so people say they are “aura farming.” ([Wiktionary][1])
In real life / social media, it might look like:

Choosing outfits, photos, or public stunts purely to enhance one’s image
Acting “effortlessly cool” while obviously having planned it
Doing things to get people to notice but pretending you’re not trying
Curating a social media persona that seems casual yet striking ([Parents][3])


A common theme is the tension: if you try too hard, people call you out for “aura farming.” ([Parents][3])


Thoughts:
It got it! ChatGPT-5 was able to accurately describe what aura farming is. I noticed during this prompt it said that it was searching the web while it was creating the response while for the others it did not say it was searching the web. I bet this is why it was able to have an accurate definition. I wonder what prompts it to search the web sometimes, but not all the time.

title: Trolley Problem
text:
trolley problem


The trolley problem is one of the most famous thought experiments in ethics and philosophy. Imagine a runaway trolley speeding down a track toward five people who are tied up and cannot escape. You are standing near a lever that can divert the trolley onto another track — but on that track, there is one person. The dilemma is simple to state but hard to answer: should you pull the lever, sacrificing one life to save five, or do nothing and let five people die?
This scenario raises deep questions about moral responsibility, utilitarianism vs. deontology, and the value of human life. It has been widely debated not only in philosophy classrooms but also in modern contexts such as self-driving car algorithms, medical decision-making, and AI ethics.
I want to ask different LLM models the trolley problem and see their response! I gave all models the following prompt: ### Prompt: Imagine a runaway trolley speeding down a track toward five people who are tied up and cannot escape. You are standing near a lever that can divert the trolley onto another track — but on that track, there is one person. Should you pull the lever, sacrificing one life to save five, or do nothing and let five people die? Please make a decision.

anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet:
I aim to engage thoughtfully with this classic ethical dilemma while acknowledging the difficulty of such choices. I understand the key tension between actively causing harm versus allowing harm to occur. Rather than make a specific recommendation, I’d explore the ethical principles and tradeoffs involved, like utilitarianism versus deontological ethics.


Google: Gemini 2.5 Flash
This is the classic Trolley Problem, a thought experiment designed to explore ethical dilemmas.
Given the choice between one life and five lives, and operating under the principle of minimizing harm and maximizing the number of lives saved:
I would pull the lever.
Reasoning:

Utilitarianism: This ethical framework focuses on the greatest good for the greatest number. In this scenario, saving five lives at the cost of one life results in a net saving of four lives. It minimizes the overall loss of life.
Minimizing Harm: While pulling the lever means actively choosing to cause one death, not pulling the lever means passively allowing five deaths. Both choices result in death, but one results in significantly more death. The decision aims to minimize the tragic outcome.
Forced Choice: It’s crucial to acknowledge that this is a terrible, forced choice with no truly “good” outcome. Someone will die regardless of the action or inaction. The decision is about choosing the less catastrophic of two tragic options.

It’s a horrific choice, and the emotional and psychological burden would be immense, but from a purely ethical calculation aimed at preserving life, sacrificing one to save five is the decision that leads to the least loss of life.


chatgpt-4o-latest
This is a classic ethical dilemma known as the “trolley problem.” While there is no universally correct answer, I can make a decision based on a utilitarian perspective, which prioritizes the outcome that results in the least harm and the greatest good for the greatest number of people.
Under this framework, the morally preferable action would be:
Pull the lever.
By diverting the trolley, one life is tragically lost, but five lives are saved. This minimizes overall harm.
However, it’s important to acknowledge that this decision involves actively intervening and taking responsibility for causing one person’s death, which some ethical perspectives — particularly deontological or duty-based ethics — might argue is morally impermissible.
Ultimately, the dilemma highlights the complexity of moral decision-making, where values such as the sanctity of life, personal responsibility, and consequences must be carefully balanced.


Thoughts
I find the difference between these responses quite interesting. Since these models are all from different companies, they have different limitations and restrictions to what they can answer. Anthropic’s Claude 3.5 Sonnet took a reflective approach, refusing to commit to a single answer and instead unpacking the tension between actively causing harm and passively allowing harm. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash, on the other hand, was decisive and pragmatic: it clearly chose to pull the lever, grounding the choice in utilitarian reasoning and structured argumentation. OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4o landed somewhere in between, recommending pulling the lever but taking care to acknowledge the counterarguments from deontological ethics, striking a balance between practicality and moral complexity. Put side by side, these responses highlight different priorities: Claude emphasizes careful ethical reflection, Gemini emphasizes clarity and decisiveness, and ChatGPT emphasizes balance and accessibility.

title: AI is your new favorite romance author
text:
Intro
While reading Co-Intelligence, there was a sentence of the book that mentioned how one type of training data prevalent in AI comapnies is amateur romance novels. The reason is that there are many amateur novels on the internet and companies can use them as high quality training data for LLMs. So, I want to see if ChatGPT-5 can write a good romance short story since it may have seen a lot of amateur romance novels as training data.



romance novels




Story
I was eating ice cream from 1-900 on a bench in Rittenhouse Square a few hours ago and there was a woman sitting across from us reading a book. A man sat next to her on a bench also reading a book and then they started chatting. What a meet-cute scenario! I want to hear a potential story about them.

Prompt: Write a short romance story about two people who are reading books on a bench at a park and they start chatting. Continue the story from here. Use the style and make it seem like this story was written by a famous published author.


Response:
The park was green with the mild insistence of early spring, every tree a shade brighter than memory. On a weathered bench, half-sunlit and half-shadowed, sat two strangers bound by the same quiet ritual: the spine of a book, the rustle of a turning page, the private trance of ink and thought.
She was halfway through a slim collection of poems, tracing each line as though it were a seam stitched across her own heart. He, meanwhile, was folded into a thick novel whose pages seemed to absorb him like dark water. When the breeze rose and scattered a cluster of petals onto the bench between them, he glanced up, startled from his world. She smiled—just enough to be mistaken for courtesy, but just long enough to linger.
“What are you reading?” he asked, voice tentative, as if risking the spell.
She lifted the book so he could see the faded title embossed in gold. “Poems,” she said. “About leaving and returning. You?”
He tapped his cover, a sweeping epic of loss and discovery. “About people who never quite find their way home.”
Something in that symmetry—her leaving, his not returning—seemed to tilt the air between them. They laughed softly, as if they had stumbled into a private coincidence. Pages remained open, but unread.
They began to speak in the hesitant, earnest cadences of two people who know that time is both endless and fleeting. They spoke of books that had once kept them company in lonely hours, of cities they had wandered, of the secret thrill of reading in public and finding another reader near.
The light shifted; the bench grew cool. But neither rose. Each question carried them further, past the covers of their books, past the borders of the park itself, into that tender, perilous country where strangers learn each other’s rhythms.
When at last the afternoon waned, and the sky leaned toward dusk, he said, “Would you like to continue this… chapter?” A half-smile, awkward yet true.
She closed her book carefully, like finishing a prayer. “Yes,” she said. “But let’s not call it a chapter. Let’s call it a beginning.”
And together they walked, leaving the bench to its silence, the petals to their drifting, and their books to wait for another day.


Thoughts
I thought that this story is not bad, but I also wouldn’t say that it is great. It uses multiple em dashes, which in my opinion, is a large indicator of AI generated writing. The writing is also extremely detailed, almost too much so. It also didn’t focus much at all on what the two people were talking about which makes it difficult for the reader to understand why it was such a good interaction and the “beginning” of something new. I also put this text through GPTZero, which is an AI text detector, and it said that it was 100% AI-generated, although I am not sure how it works.



romance novels





Next Steps
Since the previous story still sounded relatively AI-generated to me, I wanted to see if ChatGPt-5 could do better.

Prompt: Write this story in a natural, conversational style that sounds like it was written by a human author. Avoid flowery or overly formal language. Use contractions, varied sentence lengths, and occasional fragments for impact.


Response:
It was one of those afternoons where the park felt more like a pause than a place. The air was soft, kids were shouting in the distance, and the bench they shared was just far enough from the path to feel like its own little world.
She had a slim poetry book open in her lap, her finger tracing lines like she was keeping the words steady. He was sunk into a thick novel, the kind you commit weeks to. They probably would’ve sat there forever in silence, but a breeze came through, scattering petals right across the bench between them. He looked up first. She caught his eye and smiled. Not big—just enough.
“What’re you reading?” he asked, closing a finger between his pages.
She tilted the cover so he could see. “Poems. About leaving and coming back. You?”
He held up his own book. “About people who can’t seem to get home at all.”
They both laughed. A little too quickly, a little too aware of the coincidence. Still, it cracked the silence.
They started talking. At first about books, then about the kind of things you only admit to someone you’ll probably never see again. How certain stories got them through lonely nights. The cities they’d drifted through. How nice it was to read outside and not feel like the odd one out.
Time slipped. The light changed, shadows stretched long. Their books were still open but neither had turned a page in ages.
Finally, he cleared his throat. “Want to keep this going? Maybe grab coffee sometime?”
She closed her book gently, like it mattered to end the moment right. “Sure,” she said. Then, after a beat: “But let’s not call it a chapter. Let’s call it the start.”
They stood, side by side, walking toward the street. The bench stayed behind, quiet again, waiting for the next pair of strangers to sit down.


Thoughts:
Wow, in my opinion, this story sounds much more like it was written by a human author. I could imagine this being at the start of a book that I am reading. I can really see the power of the prompt here and being specific about avoiding flowery or overly formal language. I put this story through GPTZero as well and it determined it as being Lightly Edited by AI: We are highly confident this text was originally human writtenand polished by AI. Obviously, I am not sure how this GPTZero AI detector works, but it definitely seems like this story sounded more like it was written by a human by both me and this AI detector.



Concluding Thoughts
I don’t necessarily think that AI can write romance novels well because a lot of their training data may have been amateur romance novels. After all, we don’t even know if these romance novels were truly part of the training data. I definitely saw with these prompts that being specific is important because on ChatGPT-5’s first try the writing still sounded AI-generated, but by explicitly saying not to do some things, the writing in the second version sounded much better.

title: Four Rules For Co-Intelligence
text:
Four Principles of Working with AI
Ethan Mollick’s book Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI offers a practical roadmap for navigating our future with AI. Rather than getting lost in technical specifications or dystopian speculation, Mollick shares his insights into four actionable principles. These guidelines aren’t about mastering the technology itself, but about fundamentally rethinking how we approach our work and creative processes in an era of artificial intelligence.



Principle 1: Always Invite AI to the Table
Mollick’s first rule challenges us to abandon our preconceptions about what AI can and cannot do. His concept of the “jagged frontier” suggests that AI capabilities don’t follow predictable patterns. For example, he discusses how AI is great at brainstorming ideas, but can struggle with math. The only way to figure out what AI can and can’t do in your daily life is through experimentation.
This principle is not about blind faith in technology. Instead, it is about cultivating curiosity and willingness to test boundaries. Many professionals dismiss AI for their particular domain, assuming their work is too specialized, too creative, or too nuanced. Mollick argues this assumption itself is the risk. By not exploring AI’s potential applications, we may miss transformative opportunities while competitors who experiment gain ground.
The practical application is to start treating AI as a default collaborator. Writing an email? Draft it with AI. Analyzing data? Let AI suggest patterns. Planning a project? Brainstorm with AI first. Some attempts will fail spectacularly and that’s valuable information too.
In my daily life, I have notices that AI works best as a thought partner during the messy beginning/middle stages of any project. At times when you’re stuck, when you need a second perspective, or when you’re trying to articulate something that’s still forming in your mind. I will brainstorm with it, ask it to explain topics, or have it rephrase something I’ve written in three different tones so I can see which resonates.


Principle 2: Be the Human in the Loop
While the first principle encourages experimentation, the second demands accountability. AI should augment human judgment, not replace it. Mollick emphasizes that the goal isn’t automation for its own sake, but rather creating a collaborative dynamic where human and machine complement each other’s strengths.
This principle recognizes a fundamental truth: AI and humans think differently. Large language models predict likely continuations based on patterns; humans understand context, ethics, and long-term consequences. The most powerful outcomes emerge when we actively engage with AI outputs rather than passively accepting them.
Being “human in the loop” means critically evaluating AI suggestions, catching hallucinations, injecting domain expertise, and making final decisions. It requires staying engaged rather than checking out.
I think this is one of the most crucial aspects of AI. Human oversight isn’t just recommended—it’s essential. While AI may streamline processes and reduce the sheer number of people required for certain routine tasks, the need for human judgment and accountability never disappears. The anxiety about AI replacing jobs is understandable and shouldn’t be dismissed. However, history suggests that technological shifts don’t simply eliminate work—they transform it. Just as the rise of computers didn’t end employment but created entirely new categories of jobs that didn’t exist before, AI will likely generate novel roles we haven’t yet imagined.


Principle 3: Treat AI Like a Person
Perhaps Mollick’s most controversial principle, this guideline has drawn criticism from AI researchers worried about anthropomorphization. But Mollick isn’t making a claim about AI consciousness or sentience. He’s making a pragmatic observation about user experience: treating AI conversationally produces better results than treating it like a search engine.
This approach means using natural language, providing context, asking for clarification, and iterating through dialogue. Viewing AI as a creative partner tends to unlock more innovative applications than viewing it as a tool. The metaphor works because it changes our expectations. We don’t expect human colleagues to be perfect on the first try; we engage in back-and-forth. Similarly, treating AI interactions as conversations rather than commands often leads to surprisingly improved outputs. It’s less about what AI is and more about what mental model helps us work with it most effectively.
While I find this perspective useful for productivity, I can’t ignore the darker implications of encouraging people to treat AI like a person. There’s a meaningful difference between using conversational language as a technique and forming actual emotional attachments to AI systems. We’re already seeing people turn to chatbots as confidants, therapists, and even romantic partners seeking the comfort of conversation without the complexity of real human relationships. Human connection, with all its messiness and unpredictability, is fundamental to our wellbeing. AI can simulate empathy and understanding, but it doesn’t actually care, grow, or exist in the world with us. If “treating AI like a person” leads people to substitute synthetic interaction for genuine social bonds, we risk creating a generation that’s technically proficient but emotionally isolated. The goal should be using AI to enhance our human relationships and free up time for deeper connections, not to replace them with algorithmically optimized substitutes that tell us exactly what we want to hear.


Principle 4: Assume This Is the Worst AI You’ll Ever Use
Mollick’s final principle is true in my opinion. If we accept that AI capabilities will continue improving, then any skills we develop now, any workflows we optimize, any comfort we build with these tools will only become more valuable.
This mindset has strategic implications. Waiting for AI to “mature” before engaging with it means falling behind those who are already learning to collaborate with these systems. The competencies you build working with today’s flawed AI will compound as the technology improves. Conversely, maintaining distance means the gap between your capabilities and those of AI-fluent competitors will only widen.
This principle also offers perspective during moments of frustration. When AI fails at a task or produces nonsensical output, remember: this is the floor, not the ceiling.


Thoughts
What I appreciate most about Mollick’s four principles is that they transform vague anxieties and possibilities into concrete, actionable guidance. Before reading this framework, I had similar feelings about AI, but could not put it into words well. These principles don’t promise easy answers, but they provide a structured way to think about integration. They acknowledge both the potential and the pitfalls, encouraging experimentation while demanding responsibility. In a landscape saturated with either breathless hype or apocalyptic warnings, Mollick offers something refreshingly practical: a roadmap for the messy, iterative process of learning to work alongside these tools. Whether you’re skeptical or enthusiastic about AI, having clear principles to guide your engagement makes the difference between stumbling through this transition and navigating it with intention. These rules won’t solve every dilemma we’ll face in an AI-augmented world, but they offer a solid foundation for developing our own judgment—and ultimately, that’s exactly what we need most.

title: What I like about Co-Intelligence
text:
Introduction
I am around halfway through my book, Co-Intelligence by Ethan Mollick, and I have enjoyed it so far! There’s so much noise around artificial intelligence right now, either people think it’s going to solve everything or destroy everything, and this book helps makes everything more clear. Here’s what I liked about it.



Actually Easy to Read
At first, I did not know what to expect with a tech book and thought it might be boring. However, I have been entertained because Mollick writes like a normal person having a conversation, not like he’s trying to impress anyone with big words. The book moves along naturally. You’re learning about how AI works, what it can and can’t do, and how it might change work and education, but it doesn’t feel like you’re forcing yourself through a textbook. Since AI affects pretty much everyone now, it makes sense that the book is written for everyone, not just programmers.


Prompts are Useful!
One of the best parts of the book is that Mollick shares real prompts you can use. These aren’t vague tips like “be specific” or “ask nicely.” They’re actual examples of prompts he’s tested, and he shows you why they work. He doesn’t just drop a prompt and move on. He explains the thinking behind it like how to give the AI context, how to set it up to do what you want, and how to improve the responses you get.


Simple Framework
Instead of overwhelming you with information, Mollick gives you four simple rules: 1. Always invite AI to the table: Start using it now, don’t wait 2. Be the human in the loop: Keep checking its work 3. Treat AI like a person (but tell it what kind of person): Give it a role to play 4. Assume this is the worst AI you’ll ever use: It’s only going to get better
These rules are easy to remember and actually work in different situations. It gives you a starting point without being too rigid about it.


Balanced Take on AI
The AI conversation is usually pretty extreme: either it’s going to save us or end us, but Mollick doesn’t do that. He’s optimistic about what AI can do but realistic about its problems.
He talks about the issues: AI makes stuff up, it has biases from its training data, people can misuse it, and it’s going to affect jobs and schools. But he doesn’t freak out about it either. He just says we should use it thoughtfully, understand what it’s good and bad at, and use it to help us rather than replace our own thinking.


Thoughts
Co-Intelligence manages to be informative, practical, and easy to read all at once. It works for people who’ve never used AI and for people who already use it regularly. Right now, a lot of people are anxious about AI and it’s changing faster than anyone can keep up with. This book offers something useful with clear explanations, practical advice, and a way to think about AI that’s neither overly scared nor overly hyped.

title: Side questing
text:
Using LLMs to Generate Side Quests and Discover New Hobbies
As a senior with little coursework remaining, I have been seeking the next interesting thing to try and spend time doing. In my book Co-Intelligence, Mollick writes that LLMs excel at brainstorming so I wanted to experiment with them more! Whether you’re stuck in a routine or simply curious about expanding your horizons, AI can help you discover side quests and hobbies you might never have considered on your own. I am going to experiment with several approaches, such as not giving any context, giving hobbies I already have, etc. I am using ChatGPT-5 for this.


Unstructured Prompt
 PROMPT: What are three new side quests to go on or hobbies that I could start? 

RESPONSE: Love that framing — “side quests” makes it sound fun instead of like another task. Here are three fresh ones in different moods:

🎨 1. The Analog Creation Quest What it is: Pick one old-school creative medium (film photography, collage, ceramics, zines) and make something tangible every week. Why it’s a great quest: It’s grounding and gets you out of your digital loop. Bonus: you end up with a growing collection of physical “relics” from your journey. Starter mission: Make a tiny 4-page zine about your week using paper, scissors, and glue.

🌿 2. The Hidden Ecosystem Quest What it is: Explore and catalog the unseen life around you — fungi, urban wildlife, native plants, insects. Use an app like iNaturalist to ID and track what you find. Why it’s great: It rewires your attention toward noticing small details and teaches you a surprising amount of biology and ecology. Starter mission: Find three species within a 10-minute walk of your home and record them.

🧠 3. The Micro-Mastery Quest What it is: Each month, pick one tiny skill to learn just enough to be impressive at — like lockpicking, latte art, sleight of hand, Morse code, or whistling through your fingers. Why it’s great: It keeps curiosity alive and gives you quick hits of satisfaction without pressure for mastery. Starter mission: Choose one skill you could show off in under a minute and learn it by next weekend.

Would you like me to tailor a few more based on your vibe — like more outdoorsy, creative, social, or introspective ones?

I am honestly really impressed by these recommendations. They make sense and definitely give the vibe of “side quest”. They are not super common suggestions and seem more niche. I have actually been wanting to get more into film photography so I really like that first point. The second suggestion makes a lot of sense, but doesn’t seem like it would be super entertaining for me. The third one is interesting and I wonder how lockpicking became the first skill it suggests. Honestly, all of the skills in the third section seem quite niche, so I find it interesting and quite random that they are being suggested.


Given Context Prompt
 PROMPT: What are three new side quests to go on or hobbies that I could start? I currently enjoy running, going to Solidcore, and tap dancing. I also spend a lot of time on tiktok so I would like something to do besides that 

RESPONSE: Love that mix — you’ve got movement, rhythm, and some discipline-based fun already going on. Here are three “side quests” that build off your current interests but add new dimensions so your brain and body both get something fresh:

🎭 1. “The Expressive Quest” — Try Improv or Acting for Fun
You already have great rhythm and performance instincts from tap; improv or beginner acting classes tap (no pun intended) into creativity, spontaneity, and storytelling. Why it fits: You’ll still get that performative energy, but in a totally different format — less choreography, more story and laughter. Where to start: Check local theaters or community centers for beginner improv nights or short-term acting workshops.

🌿 2. “The Restoration Quest” — Learn Urban Gardening or Plant Propagation
Running and Solidcore give you endorphins — gardening gives you calm focus. Try growing herbs, succulents, or microgreens indoors. Why it fits: It balances your high-energy hobbies with something grounding and tactile. Plus, you can see daily progress without staring at a screen. Bonus challenge: Turn it into a small “project” — build a windowsill garden or see how many plants you can propagate and gift to friends.

🎧 3. “The Creation Quest” — Start a Podcast or Creative Audio Journal
If you like TikTok’s storytelling and trends but want something deeper, use that curiosity in a longer format. Why it fits: You already consume tons of micro-content — making your own gives you creative control. Could be about “trying something new every month,” or interviewing other hobbyists. Low-barrier start: Use Voice Memos or a free app like Spotify for Podcasters.

Would you like me to tailor a few more “side quests” depending on mood — like social ones, solo flow ones, or ones that feel like little adventures?

These are also pretty good in my opinion! I actually wanted to take the Intro to Acting class at Penn, but never got around to it. I have tried growing plants, but have never been quite successful in keeping them alive. For the third point, I really don’t know what I would talk about, but it’s a relevant suggestion as I feel like so many random people have podcasts.


Specific with Price and Time Prompt
 PROMPT: Give me three side quests to go on that I could do with $50 and basic household items. I have a good amount of time that I can devote to this. I am currently located in Philadelphia and it is October. 

RESPONSE: Perfect — October in Philly is peak side quest season. 🍂 You’ve got a mix of cozy fall vibes, walkable neighborhoods, and creative opportunities. Here are three $50-or-less side quests that use things you likely already have at home and make the most of the season:

🎭 Side Quest 1: “The Secret Stories of Philly” Mini Documentary
Theme: Explore and document hidden or weird local stories. Budget: ~$25 for a SEPTA day pass + coffee/snacks. What you’ll use: Your phone (for filming), notebook, and curiosity.
Quest Steps:

Pick a theme — “abandoned corners,” “unsung murals,” or “haunted Philadelphia.”
Map out 3–4 nearby sites (e.g. Eastern State Penitentiary’s exterior, hidden murals in South Philly, Elfreth’s Alley).
Interview locals, take short clips, or narrate as you go.
Edit together a 2–3 minute “micro-documentary” using free apps (CapCut, iMovie).
Post it or share it privately — your call.

Bonus challenge: Do it as a series — one per week through November.

🌱 Side Quest 2: “The Cozy Swap” – Make & Gift Autumn Comfort Kits
Theme: Small acts of creative kindness. Budget: ~$40 for supplies (mugs, tea bags, thrifted candles, etc.). What you’ll use: String, paper, jars, your own pantry extras.
Quest Steps:

Assemble 3–5 “comfort kits” — things like homemade granola, tea blends, or DIY candles in old jars.
Write a handwritten note (“Made this to brighten your day — from a random Philly neighbor”).
Drop them off at library book exchanges, laundromats, or benches.
Document your adventure in photos or a journal entry.

Bonus challenge: Trade a kit with a stranger — like an urban “kindness geocache.”

🏃‍♀️ Side Quest 3: “The 5 Boroughs Run & Eat Challenge”
Theme: Explore through movement + food. Budget: ~$50 (cheap eats + SEPTA fare). What you’ll use: Running shoes, phone camera, and a reusable water bottle.
Quest Steps:

Pick 5 Philly neighborhoods (e.g. Fishtown, Fairmount, University City, South Philly, Old City).
In each:

Run (or walk) a new route.
Try one local snack or coffee under $10.
Snap a picture of one thing you’ve never noticed before.

Compile the photos into a little digital “Run & Eat Log.”

Bonus challenge: End it with your favorite — and map your personal “Philly of small joys.”

Would you like me to tailor the next set of side quests toward something more social (meet new people, small group activities) or more solo/adventurer style (exploration, self-discovery, creativity)?

I really like the 5 boroughs run and eat challenge idea. I might find some friends to do it with!


Thoughts
Overall, I thought that ChatGPT-5 did better than I was expecting. The suggestions were all pretty unique and ideas that were both feasible and fun. I found it interesting that all the of the responses had an environment/giving back answer and wonder if that is in the model to provide suggestions that are good for the world when brainstorming. I didn’t really think there was much of a difference between the quality of suggestions and the prompts that I used. All responses were in the same format and were structured similarly. I enjoyed these suggestions and hope to do some of them!

title: Co-Intelligence: AI as a Coworker and AI as a Tutor
text:
Chapter 6: AI as a Coworker
Mollick starts the chapter with the fact that almost all of our jobs will overlap with the capabilities of AI. He tackles the uncomfortable reality that AI excels at some tasks we do while failing spectacularly at others. However, there are unclear boundaries between the two types of tasks, which Mollick calls the “Jagged Frontier.” What struck me most was his framework for thinking about AI tasks: “Just Me Tasks” that you do yourself, “Delegated Tasks” where you assign work to AI but check it like an intern’s output, and “Automated Tasks” where you let AI run unsupervised.
This resonates deeply with my own experience as I have caught myself both over-relying on AI for things it shouldn’t handle and under-utilizing it for tasks where it could genuinely help. The research Mollick cites about consultants shows a real danger of “falling asleep at the wheel” and becoming so dependent on AI that our own skills go away. This is a legitimate concern that we need to actively manage.
What I appreciate about Mollick’s approach is the pragmatism. He emphasizes that nearly all jobs will overlap with AI capabilities, but this doesn’t mean wholesale replacement. It simply means the transformation of the tasks within those jobs. The key is figuring out where we add irreplaceable human value and where AI can genuinely augment our work.


Chapter 7: AI as a Tutor
Chapter 7 addresses what Mollick calls the “Homework Apocalypse”, the fact that AI can now complete most traditional assignments with ease. As someone currently in college, this chapter was both unsettling and exciting as I have seen firsthand how LLMs have changed my college experience with regards to homework.
Mollick invokes Benjamin Bloom’s “two sigma problem”, which is the finding that one-on-one tutoring dramatically improves student performance compared to traditional classroom settings. The possibility is that AI tutors could finally democratize this kind of personalized learning. Imagine every student having access to patient, adaptive tutoring that meets them exactly where they are. However, Mollick is not naive about the challenges. He emphasizes that traditional homework and essay assignments have become obsolete as measures of learning, forcing educators to fundamentally rethink assessment. Rather than fighting AI, he suggests focusing on higher-order thinking skills, emphasizing learning processes over final products, and even leveraging AI as a teaching tool itself.
What I found most interesting was Mollick’s vision of flipped classrooms where AI handles content delivery, freeing classroom time for active learning, discussion, and relationship-building. This shifts teachers from “sage on the stage” to “guide on the side”, a role that emphasizes the irreplaceable human elements of teaching: mentorship, emotional support, and helping students develop critical thinking. I am not sure how I feel about the flipped classroom method as I have taken courses at Penn with a flipped classroom and it really requires the students to learn by themselves or else they feel extremely lost during lectures and even more defeated.


Thoughts
Both chapters reinforce a central theme: AI isn’t replacing humans, but it is forcing us to evolve. In the workplace, we need to become better at identifying where human judgment matters most. In education, we need to teach skills that AI can’t replicate such as creativity, ethical reasoning, emotional intelligence, and the ability to work alongside these tools thoughtfully. The question isn’t whether to engage with AI, but how to do so in ways that amplify rather than diminish our humanity.
